learning: If oscillation falls below 0.25 with the score at or above 213, yaw gain was the oscillation driver and kd 0.5 is worth keeping. If the score falls, kp 3.2 is too low for the s-bend and the next step is kp 3.5 with kd 0.45 rather than further reduction.
notes: Iteration 7 geometry held exactly. The only change is kp 3.5 to 3.2 to lower effective yaw gain and test whether oval oscillation (0.291 at kd 0.5) falls below 0.25. Read against the iteration 7 baseline of 213.28.
rationale: The Builder holds iteration 7's geometry exactly (wheel_track 0.09 m, five 12 mm sensors at x = -0.024 to +0.024 m and y = 0.04 m, wheel radius 0.03 m, body 0.12 x 0.18 m, mass 0.6 kg). I keep that geometry and its sensor weights [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]. The iteration 7 result of 213.28 is the baseline. Its oval steering_oscillation rose to 0.291, up from 0.2505 at kd 0.3 in iteration 6. The kd increase from 0.3 to 0.5 therefore raised oscillation, even though it lifted the score from 153 to 213 and cut slalom line loss from 2 to 1. Repeating iteration 7 would teach nothing new, so I make one controller change: kp 3.5 to 3.2. Iteration 5 showed that oval oscillation (0.277 at kp 4.0, wheel_track 0.10) tracks effective yaw gain, which is kp / wheel_track. Holding kd at 0.5 keeps the damping that produced the score gain. kp / wheel_track falls from 38.9 to 35.6. The expected result is oval steering_oscillation below about 0.25 with the score at or above 213. The risk is that less yaw gain slows the s-bend correction and raises line loss. If the score falls below 213, the controller is the cause, because the geometry is held. ki, base_speed and line_loss are unchanged.
